counterexample: Graph: s->a (weight 10), s->c (weight 1), c->a (weight 1). Standard in-place Bellman-Ford, one pass over the edge list in the order (s,c),(c,a),(s,a). After k=1 iteration: dist[c]=1, then relaxing (c,a) sets dist[a]=2, then (s,a) leaves it at 2. Node a does have a path from s with at most 1 edge (s->a, length 10), and the smallest length of a path from s to a with at most 1 edge is 10, yet dist[a]=2 after 1 iteration. So the lemma's claimed EQUALITY fails; only dist[u] <= (smallest length over paths with at most k edges) holds. The gap is exactly the one step 0012 skips: when edge (v,u) is relaxed inside iteration k+1, dist[v] may already have been improved during that same iteration, so dist[v] is not the at-most-k-edge optimum assumed by the argument.
reasoning_summary: 0001: Framing sentence announcing the lemma used in Bellman-Ford's correctness proof; no mathematical content to check, fine. 0003-0005: Statement of the lemma to be proved -- 'after k iterations, for any u having some path from s with at most k edges, dist[u] EQUALS the minimum length of a path from s to u with at most k edges'. Two hidden defects: (a) no hypothesis excluding negative cycles (with a negative cycle, minimum over WALKS with <=k edges can beat every <=k-edge path, e.g. s->a(0), a->b(-1), b->a(-1) gives dist[a]=-2 after 3 iterations while the best <=3-edge path has length 0); (b) the equality direction is false for the usual in-place implementation, only '<=' is true. Since it is the statement being proved rather than an inferential step, I record it as the source of the trouble but locate the first failing inference below. 0007: Announces induction on k; legitimate proof strategy. 0009-0010: Base case k=0. Correct and justified: dist[s]=0 equals the length of the empty path, the unique path from s to s with at most 0 edges; every other node u has no path with at most 0 edges, so the claim is vacuous there (the 'all distances are infinity' phrasing is loose but harmless). 0011: Induction hypothesis, assume the claim after k iterations and prove it after k+1. Standard and legitimate. 0012: FIRST FAILING STEP. Three separate problems. (i) It asserts 'before the (k+1)-th iteration dist[u] is the smallest length of a path with at most k edges', then treats each dist[v] as still holding that value AT THE MOMENT edge (v,u) is relaxed; in the standard single-array implementation dist[v] may already have been decreased earlier in the same pass, so dist[v]+w(v,u) can be the length of a walk with up to k+2 or more edges. This is precisely the asker's objection and it is not addressed. (ii) Consequently the claimed equality is refuted (see counterexample); what the relaxation actually establishes is the inequality dist[u] <= min length over <=k+1-edge paths, together with the invariant that dist[u] is always the length of some real s-u walk. (iii) Even under the charitable synchronous reading (compute the new array from the old one), the step only argues the '<=' direction by minimising over incoming edges; it never argues the '>=' direction (that dist[u] cannot undershoot the true optimum), which needs the no-negative-cycle assumption to convert 'minimum over walks' into 'minimum over paths'. The concluding 'this proves it!' therefore does not follow from 0009-0011. 0013, 0015: Blank separator lines, nothing to judge. 0014: Not a proof step -- the asker's objection, observing that a relaxation inside iteration k+1 can propagate a value along an edge (u,w) and thereby encode a path with up to k+2 edges. The observation is CORRECT and is exactly what invalidates the equality form of the lemma as argued in 0012 (it does not break Bellman-Ford itself, since extra propagation only makes distances converge earlier and the upper-bound form of the lemma still yields correctness after n-1 passes). 0016: Not a proof step -- restatement of the doubt about step 3; the doubt is well founded. 0017-0018: Not a proof step -- request for clarification or an alternative proof. Overall: base case and induction setup are sound, but the inductive step 0012 is unjustified and the lemma as literally stated (equality, no negative-cycle hypothesis) is false for the standard in-place algorithm, so the proof as written is invalid.
